newsitem.title: USA: FCC landmark phone-charge rules under legal assault.
newsitem.headline: FCC landmark phone-charge rules under legal assault.

text.p: The government's landmark overhaul of domestic phone charges came under legal assault Tuesday after two big phone carriers asked federal courts to overturn parts of the Federal Communications Commission rules.

The FCC last month said the new rules -- which take effect July 1 and stem from last year's big communications law -- will lower calling costs for residential and business customers who make a lot of long-distance calls.

SBC Communications Inc. and MCI Communications Corp. asked two appeals courts to set aside a key order requiring an immediate cut of $1.7 billion from the $23 billion a year long-distance carriers pay local carriers to connect calls.
Other carriers also could sue.
SBC said the FCC went too far in requiring the access charge reductions, which are expected to total $18.5 billion over five years.
Ironically, No. 2 long-distance carrier MCI said the cuts were not deep enough. MCI and rival long-distance carriers have vowed to pass along the reductions to customers.
San Antonio-based SBC also said it would ask the U.S. appeals court in St. Louis to suspend the rules while considering the request.
The Baby Bell earlier this month asked the FCC to stay the rules, saying they would put the carrier at a competitive disadvantage and that some customers would face rate hikes.
The carrier also complained the rules would let competitors lease parts of the local network -- such as call-switching devices -- without paying access charges.
The intricate web of charges have been used to keep phone service affordable, particularly in high-cost rural areas and in low-income communities.
"The FCC must find a fair and effective way to distribute the burdens and obligations of protecting affordable phone service for all Americans," SBC Senior Vice President Zeke Robertson said.

"We now must appeal to the courts in order to protect universal service and the interests of our customers, employees and shareholders and to preserve a level playing field for competitors in today's telecommunications industry."

The St. Louis appeals court last fall suspended the FCC's order opening up local phone monpolies to competition, in a victory for the Baby Bells and other local carriers. The court is expected to issue a final decision in that case soon.
MCI, meanwhile, asked an appeals court in Washington to set aside the reduction in access charges but did not seek a court-ordered stay.
In the runup to last month's rules, MCI had wanted the FCC to order an upfront reduction of some $10 billion.
Attorney Alfred Mamlet said the FCC could benefit from the two contrasting lawsuits.
"The FCC can tell the courts that it must have gotten something right because nobody's happy," he said.
Analyst Dwight Allen of Deloitte & Touche Consulting Group said the lawsuits reflect the side-effects of Congress's decision to leave vague key aspects of last year's communications law.

"This is an example of where they did not try to prescribe anything about access charges," Allen said. "In the American system, this is how we arrive at policy," he added, referring to regulators issuing rules which then face court challenge.
"Congress wanted to take back telecommunications policy from the courts," he noted wryly.
